newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa bank shares tumble, shrug off rate hike.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa bank shares tumble, shrug off rate hike.

text.p: A one percentage point hike in South Africa's central Bank rate should bring some relief to commercial banks' margins, but the sector is seen remaining under pressure amid heavy spending in the run-up to Christmas.

Banking shares on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) failed to take heart from the rate increase, announced by the Reserve Bank late on Wednesday, and tumbled along with the rest of the stock market.
Major banks on Thursday followed the central Bank's lead in pushing up its key lending rate to 17 percent from 16, hiking their prime overdraft rate by one percentage point to 20.25 percent.
"Even with a 100-basis point hike, they (banks) are still bleeding compared to where they have been," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
"It isn't really going to help particularly as we are going into the December period when the money market shortage takes some pain," he said.

Dealers said losses in banking shares were exacerbated by overall negative sentiment on the market as investors took fright over a move that would choke off domestic demand, so denting company profits.
"Banking shares have come down in line with the general market," said James Scott, an institutional trader at brokerage Frankel Pollak.
There were also concerns that banks' bad debts would deepen as consumers, hurt by already high interest rates, were squeezed even harder.

"People are already deeply in credit...you can see that just by looking at the banks' bad debts. Another one percentage point could push people even deeper into the red," another banking analyst said.

Shares in First National Bank Holdings Ltd, whose bad debt bill surged nearly 70 percent in the year to September 30, was among the heaviest losers plunging over three percent to 21.75 rand by 1000 GMT -- its weakest level in 20 months. It had since recovered a touch to trade at 22.20 rand.

By 1000 GMT shares in Amalgamated Banks of South Africa Ltd had lost 30 cents or 1.3 percent to 23.20 rand, Standard Bank Investment Corp Ltd shed 75 cents to 169 rand and Nedcor Ltd slid 50 cents to 66.25 rand.
JSE dealers said a heavy bout of arbitrage trading between the futures and spot market, which saw stocks sold off and related futures contracts bought, had further weakened banking shares.

"With the all-share index down almost 100 points the banking stocks, which make up a big component of the basket, are going to drift on the back of that," said Dominick Rey, a dealer at Investec Fergusson.
Traders and analysts said banking shares were likely to retrace some of their losses during the afternoon as futures trade quietened down and buyers appeared at the lower levels.
"Probably later this afternoon people will come back in to reassess and say this is not a bad level to get in at for the longer term," an analyst said.
